title: Why longer context windows aren’t a cure-all
excerpt: Big context windows introduce poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash that engineers must manage.
body:
A recent talk titled “Context Fails & Fixes” highlighted how the jump from ~128 000-token windows to million-token windows has not eliminated the core problems of feeding language models.

The speaker showed a model with a million-token window answer a question about the original Game Boy Pokémon Red, but the prompt contained a fabricated detail that the game was released in 1996 and was black-and-white. The model latched onto that false premise and produced a corrupted answer, proving that more context does not automatically yield correct output.

In the next few minutes the audience learned three concrete ways that larger windows can backfire: context poisoning, context distraction, and context clash. Each failure mode has a practical mitigation, and together they form a checklist for anyone building a prompt-heavy application. The sections below break down the examples, explain why the model behaves that way, and suggest concrete steps to keep the context window a help rather than a hindrance.

## Context poisoning shows up when bad facts linger

When a hallucinated or otherwise incorrect statement slips into the prompt, the model treats it as evidence it must reason over. In the Pokémon example, the hallucinated “1996 black-and-white” claim appeared early in the context, and the model repeated it throughout its answer. The source calls this failure mode *context poisoning* and notes that the model “can’t get past” the bad fact once it is embedded.

Mitigation: validate any external data before it becomes part of the prompt. A lightweight fact-checking step, such as a lookup against a trusted database, can catch hallucinations early. If validation fails, replace the suspect snippet with a neutral placeholder or omit it entirely. This keeps the context clean and prevents the model from propagating errors.

## Context distraction hurts base-knowledge recall

A larger window gives the model more material to scan, but the trade-off is that the model may start to rely on the supplied text rather than its own pre-trained knowledge.

The speaker described cases where adding a few hundred pages of background caused the model to ignore well-known facts it had learned during training. The model’s attention shifts toward the most recent tokens, and the internal encyclopedia that would normally fill gaps is sidelined. This phenomenon is labeled *context distraction*.

Mitigation: keep prompts focused and prune irrelevant material. When assembling a long context, prioritize information that the model cannot already infer. Use summarization to compress large documents into a few key points, and place essential facts near the end of the prompt where the model’s attention is strongest. By limiting noise, the model can still draw on its base knowledge when needed.

## Context confusion mixes unrelated facts

Beyond outright falsehoods, extraneous facts that do not relate to the problem can still influence the model in subtle ways. The speaker called this *context confusion*. For example, a prompt that includes a user’s personal hobby details alongside a technical question may cause the model to make assumptions about the user’s identity, subtly biasing the answer. The source describes this as “pernicious” because the influence is hard to detect.

Mitigation: separate unrelated domains into distinct prompt sections or even separate API calls. If a conversation mixes work topics with personal anecdotes, reset the context or use a fresh session for each domain. This prevents cross-contamination and keeps the model’s reasoning grounded in the relevant facts.

## Context clash arises from conflicting tool calls

Modern applications often augment language models with external tools, search APIs, calculators, or specialized agents. When the prompt contains instructions for multiple tools that contradict each other, the model can become confused about which action to take. The speaker labeled this situation *context clash*.

An example is a prompt that asks the model to “look up the latest price of Bitcoin” while also telling it to “use the cached price from yesterday.” The model may issue both calls, ignore one, or produce a mixed answer, undermining reliability.

Mitigation: design a clear hierarchy for tool invocation and ensure that instructions do not contradict each other. Define a single source of truth for each data type and enforce it in the prompt template. When multiple tools are needed, sequence the calls explicitly, first retrieve fresh data, then decide whether to fall back on cached values, so the model has an unambiguous path to follow.

## The takeaway

Treat the context window as a resource, not a cure-all. Validate facts before they enter the prompt to avoid poisoning, keep prompts concise to prevent distraction, separate unrelated domains to stop confusion, and enforce a single, non-conflicting tool-call hierarchy to eliminate clash. By applying these disciplined practices, larger context windows become a genuine advantage rather than a new source of error.
